title: Water From Rock, War With Amalek
overview: Thirsty Israelites turn on Moses in the desert and are given water from a rock, then survive a surprise attack by the Amalekites while Moses holds up his hands on a hill.

parts.label: No water at Rephidim (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The people are going exactly where they were told, yet they find no water, and their anger grows until Moses fears being stoned. Moses says that blaming him is really putting the LORD to the test, demanding proof instead of trusting.

parts.label: Water from the rock (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: Instead of punishing the people, the LORD sends Moses ahead with some leaders as witnesses to strike a rock at Horeb, another name for the Sinai region, and water pours out. Christians later read this rock as a picture of Christ, following the apostle Paul's words that the rock was Christ.

parts.label: Naming the place (v. 7)
parts.note: Moses names the spot Massah, meaning "testing," and Meribah, meaning "quarreling," so the place keeps the memory of the people's doubt and not just the rescue. Underneath the complaint was a deeper question: was the LORD with them at all?

parts.label: Battle with Amalek (vv. 8-13)
parts.note: The Amalekites, a desert tribe, attack, and a later passage says they struck the weak and tired at the back of the march. Joshua appears here for the first time leading the fighters, and Israel wins only while Moses keeps God's staff raised, which many read as a picture of prayer or of depending on God.

parts.label: A vow and an altar (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: The LORD orders a written record and vows to wipe out the memory of Amalek entirely, a harsh promise of lasting war that the text states plainly. Moses gives the altar a name meaning the LORD is his banner (a flag soldiers rallied around), though the Hebrew of verse 16 is unclear and scholars are unsure how to translate it.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to understand God's vow to blot out Amalek: some see it as just judgment on a people's specific cruelty, while others see it as reflecting the outlook of its ancient time more than God's final character.
think: What pushes people to ask "is anyone really with us or not?" when things go wrong, and what, if anything, would count as an answer for you?
